title: Rani Mukerji Will Receive an Honorary Doctorate in Melbourne Next Month. She Follows Shah Rukh Khan Into the Record Books.
excerpt: La Trobe University will confer the degree at Federation Square during the Indian Film Festival of Melbourne — only the second time a Bollywood star has been honoured this way by the Australian institution.
body:
On August 14, in the heart of Melbourne's Federation Square, Rani Mukerji will walk up to a podium and receive something no red carpet has ever given her: the letters after her name. La Trobe University will confer an Honorary Doctor of Letters on the actress during the 2026 edition of the Indian Film Festival of Melbourne (IFFM), recognising nearly three decades of work that has made her one of Indian cinema's most respected performers — and, off screen, one of its most quietly committed humanitarians. She becomes only the second Bollywood star to receive this honour from La Trobe, after Shah Rukh Khan was awarded an honorary doctorate by the university in 2019 for his philanthropic work through the Meer Foundation.

Why It Matters

Honorary degrees from international universities carry a particular resonance for Indian artists. They signal that the work has travelled — that it has registered beyond the box office, beyond the awards circuit, beyond the industry's own ecosystem. For Mukerji, whose filmography reads less like a career and more like a social register of modern India's moral questions, the recognition feels overdue. Consider the run: Black (2005), in which she played a deaf-blind woman fighting for education, required her to learn sign language and spend months studying the lives of people with disabilities. No One Killed Jessica (2011) turned a real-life miscarriage of justice into a national conversation. Hichki (2018) brought Tourette syndrome into mainstream Indian consciousness for the first time. The Mardaani films made a credible case for a female-led action franchise years before the genre caught up. And Mrs Chatterjee vs Norway (2023) — based on the true story of an Indian immigrant mother fighting Norway's child welfare system — hit so close to home for NRIs that screenings in Europe and North America turned into town halls.

The Festival

The IFFM, running from August 13 to 23, has grown into one of the world's premier celebrations of Indian cinema. The festival has historically drawn heavyweights — Amitabh Bachchan, Vidya Balan, Karan Johar, Manoj Bajpayee — and has become a key bridge between India and Australia's substantial Indian diaspora community. Mukerji herself has a deep history with the festival. She won Best Actress at IFFM in 2018 for *Hichki* and again in 2023 for *Mrs Chatterjee vs Norway*, and delivered a keynote at the Australian Parliament House during a previous edition alongside Karan Johar. The ceremony on August 14 at Federation Square — deliberately timed to coincide with Indian Independence Day celebrations in Melbourne — will be open to the public as part of the festival programme.

Beyond the Screen

The La Trobe citation specifically highlights Mukerji's work beyond cinema: humanitarian initiatives focused on children's healthcare, education, and community development for marginalised groups. It's a dimension of her career that rarely makes the entertainment pages but has been consistent across her public life. > "Through powerful performances, she has consistently championed stories that have brought conversations around women's rights, gender justice, disability inclusion and social change into mainstream cinema." — IFFM statement For the half a million Indians living in Melbourne alone, and the broader Australian-Indian community, the event carries a particular charge. When an Indian actress receives an Australian university honour at an Indian film festival timed to Indian Independence Day — in a city where dosas outnumber fish-and-chips shops in certain postcodes — it says something about how far the cultural conversation has come. Rani Mukerji has never been the loudest star in the room. She has simply, for 28 years, chosen roles that asked audiences to look at something uncomfortable and feel something anyway. Now Melbourne is looking back.
